I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Agnes had always taken pride in her work as a hotel manager, ensuring that every guest felt welcome and safe under her roof. But it's been three years since the incident, and she still can't shake off the feeling of unease that settles in every time she walks through the lobby. It was on a crowded evening, much like any other, when Agnes witnessed a violent altercation between police officers and a group of protesters outside her hotel. She had tried to intervene, but was pushed aside by an officer who shouted at her to "stay back." The image of the protester being dragged away, his face bloodied and twisted in pain, is etched in her memory like it happened yesterday. The anniversary of that event is always a difficult day for Agnes. She tries to distract herself with work, but the memories come flooding back, unbidden. This year, she found herself standing in the lobby, frozen, as a group of rowdy guests spilled out of the bar, their laughter and shouts transporting her back to that chaotic night. It's not just the crowds that trigger these flashbacks – sometimes it's a smell, like the acrid tang of tear gas, or the sound of sirens in the distance. Whatever it is, Agnes feels herself being yanked back into the past, reliving the terror she felt as she watched the police officers' brutality unfold. What frightens her most is that she no longer trusts the institutions she once believed in. The police, who were supposed to protect and serve, had instead revealed themselves to be capable of monstrous behavior. Agnes feels like she's lost her footing in a world that no longer makes sense. She wonders if she was naive to think that she could make a difference, that she could keep her guests safe from harm. This feeling of institutional failure has left her questioning everything – including herself. As the months went by, Agnes began to withdraw from her role as hotel manager. She stopped attending staff meetings, citing "health reasons," and delegated more responsibilities to her team members. Her relationships with her colleagues suffered, and she found herself eating lunch alone in her office, rather than joining them in the break room. The isolation was a self-protective measure – Agnes felt like she couldn't risk getting close to anyone again, not after what she had witnessed. But this withdrawal came at a cost. Her hotel's reputation began to suffer, and her boss called her into his office for a "chat." Agnes knew she needed to get back on track, but the thought of being in crowded spaces, or dealing with confrontational guests, filled her with dread. She felt like she was stuck in a vicious cycle – avoiding triggers that might set off another flashback, but in doing so, losing herself and her sense of purpose. It's this feeling of permanent damage that has finally brought Agnes to seek help. She hopes that therapy will allow her to reclaim some semblance of control over her life, to learn how to navigate the world without being constantly on edge. But she's also terrified – what if she can't change? What if this is who she is now – a shadow of her former self, forever haunted by the memories of that terrible night?
